title: Lesson 2: Calculating the exact speed.
section: Section 1: Displacement as a function of time
text:
Section 1: Displacement as a function of time
We have already looked at displacement-time graphs where we were told the journey someone has made (example: someone going to the shops and back home), and then using that we draw a displacement-time graph. Now we will look at how to change those graphs into an equation.

Example 1
Imagine we have Bob running a race at \(5 m/s\). If I asked you how far Bob has travelled after 5 seconds, you can simply do \(5 \times 5 = 25 m\) because we know that \(\text{Distance} = \text{Speed} \times \text{Time}\). If I asked you how far Bob has travelled after 100 seconds, you will do a similar calculation and work out \(5 \times 100 = 500\). Now if I ask you the question, “How far will Bob have travelled after ‘t’ seconds?” you know that if I ask you to calculate how far Bob has travelled at a certain time, then all you need to do is multiply the number by 5. If I say that \(x\) represents the distance, and \(t\) represents the time, then we can write the equation \[ x(t) = 5t\]
Notice that I have used \(x(t)\) on the left have side of the equation. You may not have seen this before, so be careful because this does NOT mean \(x \times t\). When you have a variable (in this case the distance) which is calculated only by using another variable (in this case the time), then we write \(x(t)\) to tell whoever is reading our work that \(t\) is the only thing used to calculate \(x\). If I also wanted to use how sloped the ground was (represented by \(s\)) to calculate how far Bob has travelled, then I would have \(x(s,t)\) because the distance Bob travels depends on both how long he has been running for, and also how sloped the ground is (if it is really steep then he might run slower).
Anyway, now that we have our equation for the displacement \(x(t)=5t\), we can plot a displacement-time graph of Bob.









Using this graph you can calculate values of \(x(t)\) without doing any Maths. All you need to do it pick your value of time, \(t\), find that value of time on the x-axis, then go up until you hit the line, then go to the left until you get to the y-axis. The value on the y-axis will give you your value for \(x(t)\). For example, if I wanted to work out the displacement after 40 minutes, you would do the following:








Figure 1: The steps showing you how to calculating the displacement for a certain time using a graph.





Now it’s your turn to have a go at some practice questions

The regular person will run at exactly \(6.5 ms^{-1}\) and the sprinter will run at exactly \(10 ms^{-1}\). Please answer the following questions:

What will the equations for displacement be for the regular person and the sprinter? (Hint: remember to include the head start for the regular person).
Who will win the race?
Draw a displacement-time graph with the regular person and the sprinter. Use the graph to explain your answer to part 3.

title: Lesson 2: Calculating the exact speed.
text:
Section 2: Non-linear displacement functions
The title of this section may look tricky, but it means that within this section we will look at displacement-time graphs which are not a straight line. For example, imagine you are stood at the top of a building and you have just dropped a ball off it. The ball will speed up as it falls to the ground (I am assuming it does not reach termial velocity). This means that a straight line for our displacement-time graph will not accurately represent the ball, because the ball does not stay at the same speed while it is falling. For our displacement-time graph, we want it to have a small gradient at the start with the gradient getting steeper towards the end. One possible graph could be:









I have chosen to use the function \(x(t)=t^2\) for this graph. This curve accuratly represents the path of the ball, but it does make calculating the speed of the ball trickier. With a straight line graph, to calculate the speed we need to pick two points and work out the gradient between them. With a straight line graph the gradient will be the same everywhere so it doesn’t matter which two points we pick. However, with a curve that has a changing gradient this will not work. We discussed last week that if we want to calculate the speed, we need to choose an interval around the point that we want which is really small. The smaller the interval then the more accurate the value of the speed. We can now use some clever Maths to calculate the speed over a really small interval so we can be really accurate.

Example 1: How to calculate speed from a non-linear displacement time graph
Imagine I have a ball falling, which can be represented by the function \(x(t)=t^2\), and I want to find the speed of the ball after 3 seconds. Your first instinct might be to do \(x(3)=3^2=9\), and say that the ball has travelled \(9m\) in \(3s\) so the ball must be travelling at \(3ms^{-1}\). However, this is not true, because this is the average speed of the ball between \(0s\) and \(3s\) NOT the exact speed of the ball at \(3s\). To find our speed of the ball at \(3s\) we need to create our interval. One of the points I’m going to use is \((3,9)\) because we have already calculated it. Then I’m going to imagine that we waiting a small amount of time after 3 seconds. I don’t know how long this small amount of time is, so I’m going to call it \(\Delta t\). This would mean our other point is \((3+ \Delta t, (3+ \Delta t)^2)\). This can be seen in the graph below:









Now that we have our interval, we can work out the speed of the ball within this interval (which is the same as the gradient of the orange line). We will do this as follows: \[\text{Gradient} = \text{Speed} = \dfrac{\text{Change in displacement}}{\text{Change in time}} = \dfrac{(3+ \Delta t )^2 - 9}{(3 + \Delta t) -3}\]
We can now simplify this fraction to get: \[ \dfrac{(3+ \Delta t )^2 - 9}{(3 + \Delta t) -3} = \dfrac{9 + 6 \Delta t + (\Delta t)^2 -9}{3 + \Delta t - 3} = \dfrac{6 \Delta t + (\Delta t)^2}{\Delta t}= 6 +\Delta t\]
Our final step requires using a limit. Last week we said that using the smallest interval possible will give the most accurate value for the speed. The smallest interval will happen when 3 is as close to \(3 +\Delta t\) as possible, and this will happen when \(\Delta t\) gets close to zero. So we can take the limit as \(\Delta t\) approaches zero: \[ \lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} 6 + \Delta t = 6 \] The above limit is shown by the diagram below. Notice how the orange line best represents the gradient (or the speed) when \(\Delta t\) is smaller.
                            
                                            
In conclusion, after 3 seconds the ball is travelling at exactly \(6ms^{-1}\).
As this is quite difficult to understand if you’ve never seen it before, then we will do another example before looking at some practice questions. However, with this example I have left parts out for you to fill in. Wherever you see ‘\(\ldots\)’ you need to fill in yourself.


Example 2: How to calculate speed from a non-linear displacement time graph
Imagine that I am an Alien who drops a ball off a building. I live on a planet with higher gravity than earth, so the ball falls to the ground quicker than on earth. The ball on this planet if governed by \(x(t)=t^3\) as it falls to the ground. What is the speed of the ball after 2 seconds?
Like in the last example, it would be useful to draw a graph. We will have ouor first point as \(x(2)=2^3=8m\) and our second point will be at \(2 + \Delta t\):









From this graph, we can work out the gradient as: \[ \text{Gradient} = \text{Speed} = \dfrac{\text{Change in displacement}}{\text{Change in time}} = \dfrac{(2 + \Delta t)^3 - 8}{(\ldots) - 2}\]
Simplifying this fraction, we will get: \[\dfrac{(2 + \Delta t)^3 - 8}{(\ldots) - 2}= \dfrac{\ldots - 8}{2 + \Delta t - 2} = \dfrac{12 \Delta t + 6 \Delta t^2 + \Delta t^3}{\Delta t}= 12 + 6 \Delta t + \Delta t^2\] Then just like the last example, we can take the limit as \(\Delta t \rightarrow 0\): \[ \lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0} (12 + 6 \Delta t + \Delta t^2) = 12 ms^{-1}\]
\(12 ms^{-1}\) is the speed of the ball governed by the equation \(x(t)=t^3\) after 2 seconds.

text:
Practice questions: Non-linear displacement functions

I have a ball which moves following the equation \(x(t)=t^2 +2t\). Please answer the following questions:

How far has the ball travelled after 4 seconds?
Work out the speed of the ball after 4 seconds.

I have two rocket ships launching off. Ship A moves by the equation \(x(t)=t^4\), and ship B moves by the equation \(x(t)=t^5\). Which ship will be faster after 30 minutes? (Hint: you do not need to do any Maths, you can answer this just be looking at the equations)

title: Lesson 2: Calculating the exact speed.
text:
Section 3: Generalising finding the speed
In the last section we looked at finding the speed at a specific point using an equation for displacement that we have. However, what if instead of trying to find the speed, we tried to find an equation for speed? We can do this using the exact same approach as what we did in the previous question.

Example 1: Finding an equation for speed
Imagine I have a ball falling according to the equation \(x(t)=t^2\). I want to find an equation which will tell me the speed of the ball at a certain time \(t\). We will call this equation \(v(t)\). We will do this example using the following few steps:

Pick two points to use
Draw a graph with these two points on
Find the gradient of these two points
Take the limit as \(\Delta t\) approaches zero

Our first step is to find two points. We want to find a point at any general time \(t\), so our first point will be the point \((t,t^2)\) (notice that this is the same as the point \((t,x(t))\) because \(x(t)=t^2\)). Then we will take another point which is close to our first point. So our second point will be \((t + \Delta t, (t+ \Delta t)^2)\). Now that we have our two points, we can draw a graph.









Using this, we can work out the gradient between our two points: \[\text{Gradient} = \text{Speed} = \dfrac{\text{Change in displacement}}{\text{Change in time}}=\dfrac{(t+\Delta t)^2 - t^2}{(t + \Delta t) - t}\]
Simplifying this fraction we will get: \[\dfrac{(t+\Delta t)^2 - t^2}{(t + \Delta t) - t}= \dfrac{t^2 + 2 t \Delta t + \Delta t^2 - t^2}{t + \Delta t - t} = \dfrac{2 t \Delta t + \Delta t^2}{\Delta t}= 2 t + \Delta t\]
Lastly, we can take the limit as \(\Delta t\) approaches zero: \[ \lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0}(2t + \Delta t) = 2t\] This gives us our final equation for speed, \(v(t) = 2t\). We can check that it works because in our other example we saw that the speed of a ball following the equation \(x(t)=t^2\) after 3 seconds was equal to \(6ms^{-1}\). Checking that with our new equation we get: \[ v(3) = 2 \times 3 = 6 ms^{-1}\] What we get with our new equation matches what we got earlier, so it is correct.


Example 2: Finding an equation for speed
This is a difficult topic, so we can look at another example. We can do the same thing for example 2 in section 2, and try to find the equation for speed where the equation for displacement is \(x(t)=t^3\). We can follow the same four steps as before. Our first step was to find two points that we can use to find the gradient between. One of our points will be \((t,t^3)\) and our other point will be \((t + \Delta t,(t + \Delta t)^3)\). Then we can draw our graph:









Our next step is to find the gradient of these two points: \[\text{Gradient} = \text{Speed} = \dfrac{\text{Change in displacement}}{\text{Change in time}} = \dfrac{(t + \Delta t)^3 - t^3}{(t + \Delta t) - t} \]
Simplifying this fraction we get: \[\dfrac{(t + \Delta t)^3 - t^3}{(t + \Delta t) - t} = \dfrac{(t^3 +3 t^2 \Delta t + 3 t \Delta t^2 + \Delta t^3) - t^3}{t + \Delta t - t}= \dfrac{3 t^2 \Delta t + 3 t \Delta t^2 +\Delta t^3}{\Delta t}= 3t^2 + 3t \Delta t + \Delta t^2\]
Then taking the limit as \(\Delta t\) approaches zero we get: \[\lim_{\Delta t \rightarrow 0}(3t^2 + 3t \Delta t + \Delta t^2) = 3t^2\]
So, when the equation for displacement is \(x(t)=t^3\), the equation for the speed will be \(v(t)=3t^2\).
In section 2 in example 2 we saw that after 2 seconds the speed of the ball would be \(12 ms^{-1}\). We can check this using our new formula and get: \[v(2)=3 \times 2^2= 3\times 4 = 12ms^{-1}\]
Now that you have seen some examples, you can have a go at some practice questions. I know that this topic is quite difficult so if you do have any questions then you can put them on the google classroom.

title: Lesson 1: Why study calculus?
text: Within this lesson, we will learn what calculus is and why we study it. We will start with an example looking at how the speed of someone running is calculated, and then we will introduce the idea of a limit. We will build up your understanding by doing lots of examples, and if you have any questions then please message on the google classroom.

title: Lesson 1: Why study calculus?
text:
Section 1: Calculating speed
For this section I have made up these numbers, this is more about the understanding than the Maths. Our first question we are going to answer is “How can we calculate the speed of something?”. This might seem obvious, because if you wanted to know the speed of someone who ran a 100 meter race in 15 seconds, then you would do the following calculation: \[ Speed=\dfrac{Distance}{Time}=\dfrac{100}{15}=6.67ms^{-1}\] This means that if Bob did run a 100 m in 15 s, then his average speed would be 6.67 m/s. However, we do know that he will not have travelled the entire race at this speed. During the start of the race he will be accellerating to his top speed, and he will be at his top speed in the middle of the race once he has fully accellerated. This means during the start he will be travelling less than 6.67 m/s and at the middle of the race he will be travelling quicker than 6.67 m/s. So how would we calculate the speed of the Bob once he is exactly 15 m into the race? As we are dealing with distance, it makes sense to change the distance that we are measuring over. Instead of working out his speed for the entire race, we can work out his speed for the first 30 m, as this will give us a more accurate value of how fast he is travelling at 15 m. If it took Bob 8 s to run the first 30 meters, then we will get: \[ Speed = \dfrac{Distance}{Time}=\dfrac{30}{8}=3.75ms^{-1} \] As you can see, this 3.75 m/s is slower than 6.67 m/s which is exactly what we expected. We can also decrease the distance we measure on even more, for example we can measure the time it takes Bob to run between 10 m and 20 m. Measuring the time it takes Bob to run between 10 m and 20 m will give a more accurate value for the speed Bob is running at when he is exactly 15 m into the race. This can be seen in figure 1.








Figure 1: A diagram showing a 100m race track, with the 15m mark labelled.





Now we can take a step back and think about what is happening. As we decrease the distance that we measure over, then the value of the speed becomes more accurate. So we want to measure over the smallest distance possible in to find the most accurate value for the speed of the person. Now we can have a go at some practice questions.

Practice questions: Calculating speed

Imagine a cyclist in a 10000 m race. I want to find out their speed at exactly halfway into the race. Which distace to measure over would give me the most accurate value of their speed? Please choose one of the three options.

Between 3000m and 6000m
Between 4500m and 9000m
Between 4000m and 6000m

At the 2008 Olympics Usain Bolt broke the world record for the 100 m sprint. Figure 2 below shows the times that Bolt crossed each 10 m interval. Use this data to answer the following questions:

What was Bolt’s average speed for the entire race?
Use two different intervals to calculate Bolt’s speed at the 35 m mark, explain why you have got different answers.
Calculate Bolt’s speed at 75 m using the interval which would give you the most accurate answer.

We have mentioned how a measuring the time over a smaller distance gives a more accurate value for the speed of a person in a race. However, can you explain the practical difficulty of measuring over an extremely small distance. Such as between 9.99 m and 10.01 m









Figure 2: A table showing the times Usain bolt crossed each 10 m interval in his record breaking 100 m sprint.

title: Lesson 1: Why study calculus?
text:
Section 2: Displacement time graphs
Note that for this section I am using displacement and velocity instead of distance and speed. For those of you who have not studied the differences between distance and displacement (or speed and velocity), then you can think of them as the same thing and you will still be able to follow along. You should now have a good understanding of how speed is calculated, now we can look at what this means on a graph. Displacement time graphs are commonly used to solve problems using speed. Displacement is displayed on the y-axis of the graph and time is displayed on the x-axis of the graph. For example, if I walked into university, then sat through a lecture and then got the bus back home, my displacement time graph would look something like the following:









From graph 1 we can see a few things. The y-axis tells us that the University is 1km away from my house, as the line becomes horizontal at the 1km mark. The x-axis is telling us that it has taken me 30 minutes (or 0.5 hours) to walk into University, then spent 1 hour at University, then it took me around 20 minutes to get home on the bus. For a displacement time graph, the gradient of the graph represents the velocity. This can be seen because the gradient of the graph when I take the bus is steeper than the gradient of the graph when I walk, which implies that I am moving quicker when I’m on the bus, and slower when I’m walking. We can also see that the gradient of the graph is zero for the duration of my lecture, which means that I am not moving while watching my lecture. The last comment I want to make about this graph is that it is not perfectly accurate. We can see that the gradients of each portion of the graph is a straight line, which implies that I am moving at a constant velocity. We know this is not true because in real life you may have to stop or speed up for certain reasons (i.e. while I’m walking I may have to stop at traffic lights or while I’m on the bus the bus might wait at a bus stop). From this graph, there are two key takeaways:

The gradient of a displacement time graph represents the velocity
The steeper the gradient, then the greater the velocity


Practice questions: Displacement time graphs

This question uses graph 2. Graph 2 shows a displacement time graph of Bolt’s 100 m world record. Using the graph, answer the following two questions:

Explain why the gradient of the graph between 10 m and 100 m is a lot steeper than the gradient of the graph between 0 m and 10 m.
Explain how you would work out the displacement of Bolt at around 60 m into the race.

This question uses graph 3. I go for a trip on my bicycle. I cycle for 20 minutes to go to the shops, then I cycle for 10 minutes to my friends house, and I then cycle all the way home. My trip can be shown using graph 3. Please answer the following 3 questions:

How long did I spend at my friends house? Answer in hours.
Can you calculate my speed for when I cycled back home from my friends house? As this is speed I need the answer as a positive number, so if you get a negative answer then get rid of the negative sign and just submit that number.
After travelling 2km on the way to the shops, I got a puncture and had to get off my bike to repair it. I repaired the puncture in 5 minutes and got back on my bike to continue my journey. I still got to the shops 20 minutes after leaving my house. What does the new graph look like? (You can draw the new graph or just describe it).




















Now you may have realised that with all of the calculations so far we are still using two values of the distance to measure the time over and using that to calculate speed. You may ask yourself the question “Is it possible to only using one value of the distance to calculate the speed?” and you can do this using calculus! However, before we look at that, we need to understand what a limit is.

title: Lesson 1: Why study calculus?
text:
Section 3: What is a limit?
In Maths, a limit is used to say that if we have some number x that is getting closer and closer to another number y , then x=y . For example, if we have some number x , that keeps getting closer and closer to the number 3, then we will write: \[ \lim_{x \rightarrow 3} x = 3 \] One way that I like to think of limits is by thinking of an ant on a number line. As you can see from figure 3, the ant is starting from the left and it will keep moving to the right until it reaches the number 3, then it will stop.








Figure 3: An ant moving slowly along a number line until it reaches the number 3





For this example it does not matter if the ant starts at the number -1 and move to the right (like it has in the diagram), or if the ant starts at the number 6 and moves to the left, as it will always finish at the number 3. There can be times when the value of the limit does depend on whether your increasing or decreasing with your value of x (if your ant is moving to the left or to the right). One of the practice questions I have included for this section shows this and I have included it to challenge you so do not worry if you struggle with it, as we will talk about it when we have the lesson.
All of that aside, most limits I will show you can simply be solved be a direct substitution. For example, if I have the following: \[ \lim_{x \rightarrow 2} x^2-4x+5 \] Then all I need to do to solve this is substitute in x=2 , which will give me: \[ \lim_{x \rightarrow 2} x^2-4x+5 = (2)^2-4(2)+5=4-8+5=1\]
A more visual understanding of this would be to picture the ant moving along the curve of the graph. For example, below shows the graph of \(y=x^2-4x+5\):









From this curve, we can imagine that an ant is stood to the right of two and to the left of two, with both ants making their way towards 2 but they’re walking along the curve. This can be shown in the diagram below, where the arrows represent the direction that the ants are moving:








Figure 4: A graph showing ants moving along a curve.





From this curve it is easy to see what will happen to the ants. Both ants will meet at \(x=2\) where \(y=1\), just like what we saw in the previous example. Remember this technique when solving practice question 3.
We have looked at limits where we are converging to a number, but what happens when we are going off to infinity. Unfortunately, as infinity is not a number we cannot simply substitute it into an formula and solve it, so instead there are two main ways that we solve limits with infinity. Suppose I wanted to find out what \(lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} -x^3+5x^2-x-6\) is equal to. The first way would be to draw a graph:









Just by looking at the graph, we can see that it looks like as \(x\) gets bigger, then \(y\) gets smaller meaning that if \(x\) is going off to infinity, then \(y\) is going to negative infinity. We can confirm this by trying the second method. I said that we cannot substitute infinity into the formula (as infinity is not a number), however we can still just substitute in really big numbers to see what happens. We can substitite in 1000, 10000 and 100000 into \(-x^3+5x^2-x-6\) to see what it gives us:
\[ -(1000)^3+5(1000)^2-(1000)-6=-995001006\] \[ -(10000)^3+5(10000)^2-(10000)-6=-9.9950001001 \times 10^{11}\] \[ -(100000)^3+5(100000)^2-(100000)-6= -9.999500001 \times 10^{14}\]
From this, we can see that when we substitute in larger values of \(x\) then the \(y\) values decrease by larger amounts, meaning that \(\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} -x^3+5x^2-x-6 = - \infty\).

title: Lesson 1: Why study calculus?
text:

title: Lesson 1: Why study calculus?
text:
Notes from the lesson on 9/6/2026
Within our previous lesson we managed to start looking at some of the content within section 1. During the lesson I found that some of my explanations had not been as good as planned. I am writing this section just to help with some of the questions as I found that there was some confusion.

How to calculate speed
The speed of a person is defined as follows: \[ Speed = \dfrac{\text{Change in distance}}{\text{Change in time}}\] We know that the ‘Change in distance’ is going to be the length of the interval, and the ‘Change in time’ is going to be how long it took the person to go through the interval. This means we can write: \[ Speed = \dfrac{\text{Change in distance}}{\text{Change in time}} = \dfrac{\text{Distance at the end - Distance at the start}}{\text{Time at the start - Time at the end}}\] Note that when I say ‘at the start’ and ‘at the end’ I mean ‘at the start of the interval’ and ‘at the end of the interval’.


Example question
If we are trying to solve part c of the 2nd question in section 1 then we can use this formula. We know that the smallest interval around 75 m is going to give the the most accurate value for the speed. Knowing this we will consider the 70 m to 80 m interval. Now we can use the formula for speed: \[ Speed = \dfrac{\text{Distance at the end - Distance at the start}}{\text{Time at the start - Time at the end}} = \dfrac{80 - 70}{7.96 - 7.14} = \dfrac{10}{0.82} \approx 12. 20 ms^{-1}\]


Common mistakes
During the lesson some students had a go at solving part c of the 2nd question in section 1 and they made mistakes. Mistakes are brilliant because it shows that you are learning and it also helps me as I will be able to explain it better to future students. One of the mistakes made was calculating the speed for the interval 0 m to 75 m. This can be done by working out the speed for the interval 0 m to 70 m and the speed for the interval 0 m to 80 m, and then taking an average of the two. That calculation would be done like this: \[ \text{Speed for the interval 0m to 75m} = \dfrac{\text{Speed for the interval 0m and 70m}+ \text{Speed for the interval 0m and 80m}}{2} = \dfrac{\frac{70}{7.14}+\frac{80}{7.96}}{2} \approx 9.925 ms^{-1} \] The problem with this is that we are using an interval which is 75 m, so we are still including the start of the race where Bolt will be running slower. Therefore, this method will not produce the most accurate value for Bolts speed at 75 m. I have included a diagram below to help explain this:
